header:
Date: 2026-11-18
Time: 15:00 - 15:52 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Jesse Marlow (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Daniel Ortiz (CTO, Rivermark), Maya Chen (Head of MLOps, Rivermark), Liam O'Neill (Infra Lead, Rivermark)
Recording: yes
Location: Zoom
transcript:
00:00 Jesse: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, this is Jesse from Redwood, I have Priya here, our systems engineer. How's everyone doing?
00:08 Daniel: Hi Jesse, good thanks. Maya and Liam on our side. We have about 50 minutes, mainly want to understand Dedicated offering and how we can get predictable throughput for our fraud and risk models.
00:17 Priya: Awesome. We'll run through architecture, sizing, isolation options (VPC, on-prem), burst and autoscale patterns, and then take your constraints. Feel free to jump in.
00:28 Maya: Great, quick context: we run a mix of real-time scoring (latency sensitive, 50-200ms target) and batch rerank jobs. Models are a mix of open transformer models and a few fine-tuned variants, roughly 7B-13B. We need data isolation, SOC2 compliance, and integration with our KMS.
00:45 Liam: Also — and this is important — we need to be sure that spikes during business hours (end-of-day settlements) won't blow up our bills. We want reserved capacity but also burst. What does Redwood recommend?
00:58 Jesse: Good, that's exactly the use case for Dedicated. We provide reserved GPU pools with predictable throughput; you can configure burst capacity to absorb short spikes. Priya, want to go into technical detail?
01:08 Priya: Sure. Dedicated is essentially a reserved cluster for your account. You pick GPU types and counts; we provision a pool and route requests to it. For burst, you can enable a burst pool that's billed differently and subject to tenant policies. It can be auto-enabled for short spikes or manually triggered.
01:26 Maya: Are burst instances shared across customers? We need isolation — can't have noisy neighbors.
01:30 Jesse: For Dedicated we do tenant-isolation at the GPU pool level. Burst can be configured two ways: either from your reserved tenant capacity (we autoscale within your pool) or via a shared burst capacity for committed customers with isolation guarantees. Priya?
01:42 Priya: Right — by default burst uses your own reserved headroom if you've provisioned it. For additional short-term headroom we offer a dedicated burst cluster option (reserved + buffer) or access to a shared burst pool but only with strict tenancy controls; we can discuss SLA tradeoffs.
01:55 Daniel: Can you explain the autoscaling profile — how fast is scale up/down and how does caching affect latency?
02:03 Priya: Autoscale depends on the model's cold-start time and the GPU type. For transformer inference with KV cache reuse, cold start is low if you keep warm containers; typical scale-up to a new GPU node is in the 30-90s range. We do warm pools and smart routing to avoid cold starts for frequent traffic. Caching — prefix/KV caching — really reduces per-token compute for repeated prefixes, which helps latency and cost.
02:25 Liam: So for our 50-200ms SLO for small prompt scoring, is that realistic on 13B?
02:30 Priya: It is, with the right GPU selection and batching rules. Example: A4 or H100 class GPUs with aggressive batching can hit sub-200ms for single-shot scoring at 13B with minimal tokens, but throughput and concurrency planning matters. We'll estimate more precisely after you share traffic.
02:44 Maya: About networking — we need VPC peering, SAML SSO for console, and KMS integration. Also audit logs forwarded to our SIEM.
02:54 Jesse: Those are standard in Private, but for Dedicated we support VPC connectivity, SSO via SAML, and KMS integrations for key material. Audit logs and long-term retention are available as an add-on. We'll attach our SOC2 and architecture docs.
03:08 Daniel: What's the difference between Dedicated and Private here? We're leaning Dedicated, but compliance might push us to Private.
03:15 Jesse: Dedicated is hosted by Redwood but provides tenant isolation and VPC options — you still use our control plane. Private gives you a customer-managed control plane and optionally on-prem deployments for stricter regulatory needs. Dedicated tends to be faster to onboard with similar isolation for most audits, but Private is for locked-down environments.
03:31 Maya: Ok. On onboarding: we'd want a pilot with baseline benchmarks against our production models. Can you support bringing our model checkpoints?
03:38 Priya: Yes. We can accept model artifacts and run onboarding benchmarks in a staging Dedicated cluster. We recommend a 1-week baseline run that mimics peak patterns to size and tune batching/quantization. We can also explore quantized variants if that helps cost.
03:51 Liam: Any limitations on custom kernels or very bespoke model ops?
03:55 Priya: We support many model families and can add custom kernels in collaboration, but custom kernel work is scoped as professional services for risk and testing. For normal fine-tunes and adapters it's straightforward.
04:05 Daniel: Pricing — we prefer a committed monthly for predictability. How are bursts billed?
04:10 Jesse: Committed reserved capacity is billed as a monthly commit; burst usage beyond that is billed at a higher per-hour rate. Alternatively you can purchase a dedicated burst buffer to reduce burst unit rates. We'll send a pricing sheet with examples.
04:22 Maya: We also want to understand failure modes — if your region has capacity issues, do we automatically fall back to smaller models or different regions?
04:30 Priya: We support policy-based routing: fallbacks to compatible model variants in the same pool or another region. You can set cost vs latency policies. If region capacity is exhausted we can route to a pre-approved fallback (e.g., 7B family) or failover to another region per your policy.
04:43 Daniel: Good. About latency percentiles — we need p99 under 300ms for scoring. How do you measure that?
04:49 Priya: We expose token-level and request-level traces in Redwood Console with percentiles per route and model. You can also ship traces to your tracing backend. We can instrument the pilot to collect p50/p95/p99.
05:00 Maya: Security questions: do you allow customer-managed keys for model artifacts and for inference encryption in transit at rest?
05:06 Jesse: Yes — KMS/HSM integration is supported for data at rest; in transit is TLS. For very strict key control we have Private with customer-managed control plane and HSM integrations.
05:16 Liam: What about model data residency — logs, prompts — can those be routed to our region only?
05:22 Priya: Yes, you can restrict storage region for logs and data; we have region controls. For Dedicated we can ensure logs remain in the region and forward audit logs to your SIEM.
05:32 Daniel: Operationally, who is the on-call for incidents during pilot?
05:36 Jesse: For Dedicated, Redwood provides 24/7 platform support; for pilot we provide an onboarding SE plus an escalation path. For enterprise contracts you can add premium SRE support.
05:44 Maya: Ok, let's dive into workload specifics — our scoring traffic is about 300 req/s in peak with average 1-2 tokens per request and occasional batch jobs processing 100k rows overnight. We also have scheduled end-of-day surges that triple traffic for ~15-40 minutes.
06:02 Priya: That burst pattern is fairly common. For that, we typically recommend 1) reserved baseline sized for steady-state 300 rps with headroom, 2) a dedicated burst buffer sized to handle the 3x spikes for 40 minutes, or 3) autoscale with warm nodes and quick scale-up. Each has cost tradeoffs.
06:20 Jesse: Example math: if steady 300 rps fits on N GPUs, you might reserve N+20% for headroom and buy a 30-60 minute burst buffer to avoid provisioning full-time. We'll run detailed numbers.
06:31 Daniel: Will autoscaling introduce a lot of cold starts and latency blips?
06:35 Priya: Potentially — but we mitigate with warm pools and pre-warm policies. Cold start blips are usually in the tens of seconds for new instances; for strict p99 SLOs we recommend at least some pre-warmed capacity.
06:47 Liam: Do you support token-based caching for repeated prefixes — our chatbot front-end hits similar system prompts a lot.
06:53 Priya: Yes, prefix and KV caches are supported. That can drastically reduce cost for chat patterns where prompts share prefixes. We'll help tune cache TTLs.
07:02 Maya: We use internal models for sensitive PII redaction — can Redwood run custom pipelines (pre/post processing) in the inference path?
07:09 Priya: You can implement pre/post-processing either client-side or as middleware in Redwood with function/tool calling. We support running lightweight transforms and hooking to postprocessors; heavier custom logic can be proxied.
07:21 Daniel: About deployment lifecycle — we want canary rollouts and A/B for model variants. Is that built-in?
07:26 Jesse: Yes, Redwood Console supports rollouts, canaries, A/B, and automatic fallback policies. You can pin routes to model version and do gradual rollouts.
07:35 Maya: For the pilot we want to run three variants: 13B baseline, 13B quantized, and a 7B fallback. Can Redwood host multiple variants in the same Dedicated pool?
07:44 Priya: Yes, you can host multiple model variants; runtime will pick kernels and schedule. We can also move less-used variants to lower-cost nodes. For quick routing and fallbacks it's straightforward to set route policies.
07:57 Daniel: Good. About SLAs — what uptime/latency SLAs do you offer?
08:02 Jesse: For Dedicated we provide SLA-backed uptime and latency targets in enterprise contracts; baseline SLAs for hosted tiers are lower. We'll include SLA targets in the proposal.
08:11 Liam: We need auditability for DSARs and logging if a regulator requests prompts. How long are logs retained?
08:18 Priya: Retention is configurable; default is 90 days, can extend to 1 year or custom retention and export. PII controls and redaction can be applied at ingest.
08:28 Maya: Ok I have a list of compliance items we'll send. Will Redwood sign a DPA and security addendum?
08:33 Jesse: Yes, we execute standard DPAs and security addenda; for higher-risk controls we can negotiate. We'll share legal contacts and our SOC2 report.
08:44 Daniel: Onboarding timeline — if we decide now, how fast can we go?
08:48 Jesse: Typical Dedicated onboarding is 2-6 weeks depending on pilot complexity. For a basic pilot with our staging cluster we can start within 2 weeks; full production rollouts take longer.
08:58 Maya: For the pilot we'll need credentials and a test namespace.
09:02 Priya: We'll create a staging namespace; SSO set up and VPC peering takes a few days once we have network info.
09:09 Daniel: Let's talk about GPU choices — we currently use A100 in our infra. Any benefits to switching?
09:15 Priya: A100/H100 both good — H-class has improved perf for some kernels, A-class is cost-effective. For 13B inference H100 can give lower latency; we'll recommend after perf estimates.
09:27 Liam: Do you support tensor parallelism and multi-GPU sharding for large models?
09:31 Priya: Yes, multi-GPU sharding is supported for models that need it. For 7-13B usually single-GPU fits, but larger families use sharding.
09:40 Daniel: Ok, any blockers we should know now?
09:43 Maya: Compliance questionnaire and region controls — we need those answered quickly. Also we want an estimate of monthly committed cost vs burst-only.
09:51 Jesse: We'll send a pricing sheet with examples (steady reserve vs reserve+burst). Also we'll attach our security pack and a template SOW for pilot.
09:59 Priya: I'll take the lead on perf estimate once Maya shares the sample traffic. We can model concurrency, batching, and expected token throughput.
10:07 Daniel: For the pilot's baseline benchmark, can you run our exact model with our checkpoints?
10:11 Priya: Yes, send model artifacts via our secure upload link and we can run it in staging. We'll need expected prompt distributions too.
10:19 Maya: We'll share artifacts and traffic by tomorrow.
10:22 Jesse: Great. Quick recap of next steps then...
10:25 Daniel: Before that — one more question on failover: if Dedicated cluster has a hardware failure, what's the RTO?
10:30 Priya: Our design replicates control plane and we have replacement capacity; RTO depends on failure but typical recovery for instance replacement is minutes to an hour. For critical paths we recommend multi-region fallback policies.
10:40 Jesse: OK recap: Jesse to send pricing and contract template; Priya to run GPU sizing/perf estimate; Rivermark to provide traffic/profile and model artifacts; schedule pilot kickoff for week of 2026-11-30.
10:50 Maya: Sounds good. We'll also send the compliance questionnaire.
10:53 Daniel: Thanks Jesse, Priya. We'll review and get the info over.
10:56 Jesse: Thanks all, talk soon.
11:00 [meeting ends]
